previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: An elderly male with a history of COPD, CAD s/p CABG, CVA, esophageal stricture, and active alcoholism was admitted for septic shock and multifocal pneumonia following acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring intubation. He presented with severe dyspnea, aspiration, and septic shock, with labs showing lactic acidosis and acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressors, and mechanical ventilation. A sputum culture grew Enterobacteriaceae, prompting targeted therapy. After stabilization, he was extubated and transitioned to the medical floor. Due to persistent dysphagia and aspiration on swallow studies, an NJ tube was initially placed, but due to recurrent clogging, a percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy (PEJ) tube was ultimately placed for long-term nutrition. He improved clinically, with resolution of infection and kidney function, and was discharged to extended care for rehabilitation with plans to reassess swallowing and support alcohol cessation.

Hospital course:
# Fevers: Given the patient's previous history of aspiration 
pneumonia and findings of consolidation on chest xray, he was 
initially treated for an aspiration vs. healthcare associated 
pneumonia. In addition, he had a cellulitis around his G-tube 
site. He was started on IV vancomycin, cefepime, and flagyl. The 
following day he seemed to have baseline respiratory status and 
was not felt to have a pneumonia. He was discharged on bactrim 
antibiotics to cover his cellulitis. 

# G-tube: The patient stated that he had not used the tube for 
weeks and was able to tolerate a PO diet without difficulty. He 
wanted the tube removed. We got a speech and swallow evalulation 
who were unable to adequately evaluate his swallowing at 
bedside, and they recommended a video swallow. However, the 
patient stated that even if the video swallow demonstrated 
aspiration events, he would still eat by mouth and would not use 
the G-tube. We explained the risks associated with aspiration, 
such as pneumonia and death. The patient stated that he 
understood these risks and wanted the tube removed anyway. These 
risks were also discussed with the patient's health care proxy, 
his brother ___. The patient elected to have the tube 
removed by interventional radiology as an outpatient.

# COPD: No active issues. Albuterol/ipratropium nebs, 
fluticasone inhaler

# Hyponatremia: The patient had sodium of 131 on admission, 
which improved to 135 the following day. The patient has chronic 
hyponatremia, with sodium usually in the low 130s. He should 
follow up with his primary health care provider.

# Anemia: The patient has chronic anemia, previously attributed 
to his alcoholic use. However, his anemia on admission was 
microcytic and his iron studies showed iron deficiency. He 
should follow up with his primary care physician about starting 
iron supplementation and getting a colonoscopy.

# Knee/ankle pain: The patient had left knee and hip pain during 
admission. He stated that he previously had this pain but had 
not had it for a while. The pain was controlled with tylenol. 
The patient should follow up with his primary care physician if 
the pain does not improve.

chronic process, with a new area of patchy opacification seen in the right
upper and mid lung field.  No pleural effusion or pneumothorax is seen.  No

IMPRESSION:

New patchy opacification in the right upper to mid lung field concerning for

INDICATION:  History of G-tube in ___, now with fever, diffuse abdominal pain
and presence of intra-abdominal abscess, who presents for evaluation.

COMPARISONS:  CT abdomen and pelvis from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  ___ MDCT images were obtained through the abdomen and pelvis after
the administration of IV contrast.  Multiplanar reformatted images in coronal
and sagittal axes were generated and reviewed.

FINDINGS:

The bases of the lungs demonstrate mild atelectasis as well as chronic
appearing interstitial changes.  

The liver is normal without evidence of focal lesions or intrahepatic biliary
ductal dilatation.  The gallbladder demonstrates cholelithiasis without
evidence of cholecystitis. The spleen is homogenous and normal in size.  The
adrenal glands bilaterally are normal.  Note is made of multiple hypodensities
within the kidneys bilaterally, the largest on the right measuring 2.8 cm x
2.8 cm, series 2, image 42, compatible with a simple renal cyst.  The largest
on the left measures 1.9 cm x 1.5 cm, series 2, image 40, also compatible with
a simple renal cyst.  Pancreas appears atrophic, otherwise is unremarkable. 
There is no pancreatic duct dilatation.

Small hiatal hernia is present. There is a percutaneous G-J tube which enters
the body of the stomach and appears to terminate in the jejunum.  There is no
evidence of an intra-abdominal abscess. There is no retroperitoneal or
mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There is no intra-abdominal free fluid or free
air.

There are moderate-to-severe atherosclerotic calcifications along the course
of the abdominal aorta, iliac arteries, and mesenteric arteries. Retroaortic
left renal vein is incidentally noted.

Note is made of extensive colonic diverticulosis without evidence of
diverticulitis.  The appendix is visualized and is normal.

CT PELVIS:  The urinary bladder is unremarkable.  There is no pelvic free
fluid.  No pelvic wall or inguinal lymphadenopathy is identified.  The
prostate and seminal vesicles are unremarkable.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  Partially visualized sternal wires appear to be intact. 
No lytic or blastic lesions concerning for malignancy are identified.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence of an intra-abdominal abscess.  No acute intra-abdominal
abnormalities identified.

2.  Appropriate course of the G-J tube terminating in the mid jejunum.

3.  Cholelithiasis without evidence of cholecystitis.

4.  Extensive diverticulosis.

LUMBAR SPINE RADIOGRAPH

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ male with history of CVA and lower extremity

TECHNIQUE:  AP and lateral radiographs of the lumbar spine were obtained.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS:  There is moderate degenerative change within the lumbar spine with
